name: Paro & Thimphu
tagline: Himalayan valleys of dzongs, prayer flags and cliffside monasteries.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Spring and autumn are clear and mild; late September to November offers the crispest Himalayan views. A daily sustainable-tourism fee applies year-round.

ourTake.lede: Don't rush Bhutan, the tariff means every day costs, so linger rather than cramming dzongs. Paro and Thimphu are the gentle entry; save your legs and lungs for the climb to Tiger's Nest and do it early, ideally acclimatised after a day or two. Time a trip to a tshechu if you can, but even outside festival season the valley walks and farmhouse dinners are the real Bhutan.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Tiger's Nest, empty valleys and Aman-grade calm.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife, shopping or a beach.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Amankora
credentials: MICHELIN Key 2025, Two Keys (Bhutan's top tier)
Aman, the group's flagship Bhutan collection
items.description: Aman's circuit of five intimate lodges across Bhutan's valleys, you journey lodge to lodge like a pilgrimage, and it remains the country's defining luxury experience.

items.name: Six Senses Bhutan
credentials: MICHELIN Key 2025, One Key
Prix Versailles World Award, Best Hotel Design
items.description: Five architecturally distinct lodges, the Thimphu hilltop, Paro's 'stone ruins', Punakha's flying farmhouse, bound into one wellness-led circuit.

items.name: Gangtey Lodge
credentials: MICHELIN Key 2025, Two Keys
Condé Nast Traveler Gold List
Travel + Leisure Global Design Awards 2014
items.description: Twelve farmhouse suites above the Gangtey monastery and the black-necked-crane valley, Bhutan's most decorated single lodge, and its most romantic.

items.name: COMO Uma Paro
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018, among the world's best hotels
COMO Hotels & Resorts
items.description: COMO's serene hillside house over the Paro valley, ten minutes from the airport, and home to Bukhari, the country's best-known table.

items.name: Pemako Punakha
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Hot List 2024, best new hotels in the world
items.description: Bill Bensley's theatrical tented palace on the Mo Chhu, twenty-one pool villas, five dining venues, pure Punakha extravagance.

items.name: andBeyond Punakha River Lodge
credentials: DestinAsian Luxe List 2024, best new hotels & resorts in Asia
items.description: andBeyond's first owned lodge in Asia, six canvas-and-timber tented suites on the banks of the Mo Chhu, light-footprint safari luxury brought to the Himalaya.

items.name: Zhiwa Ling Heritage
credentials: Genuine standing, Bhutan's landmark locally-owned heritage hotel, one of the few five-stars in Bhutanese hands
items.description: An owner-built Bhutanese heritage house, hand-carved timber, painted murals, and a shrine of 450-year-old restored monastery wood, with Tiger's Nest in view.

items.name: COMO Uma Punakha
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018, voted the best hotel in Asia
items.description: COMO's small, calm eleven-room lodge above the Punakha valley, intimate, unhurried, with the river valley laid out below.

items.name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
credentials: Bhutan's most iconic pilgrimage and hike
items.description: Bhutan's defining image: a 17th-century monastery clinging to a sheer cliff 900 metres above the Paro valley, reached by a 4-to-5-hour round-trip climb through pine and prayer flags. Guru Rinpoche is said to have flown here on the back of a tigress; the ascent is the emotional centre of any Bhutan trip and doable at a gentle multi-generational pace with horses to the halfway teahouse.

items.name: Rinpung Dzong (Paro Dzong)
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
items.description: The 'Fortress on a Heap of Jewels' rises in whitewashed tiers above the Paro river, a working seat of monks and district administration and the stage for the springtime Paro Tshechu. The covered cantilever bridge below is one of the most photographed sights in the kingdom.

items.name: Ta Dzong (National Museum of Bhutan)
credentials: National museum of Bhutan
items.description: A round former watchtower above Paro Dzong, now holding over 3,000 works spanning 1,500 years of Bhutanese art, thangkas, bronzes and ritual objects. It gives multi-gen travellers the cultural grounding that makes the rest of the trip legible.

items.name: Kyichu Lhakhang
credentials: Among Bhutan's oldest temples (7th century)
items.description: One of the oldest and most sacred temples in Bhutan, said to be among 108 built by a Tibetan king in the 7th century to pin down a demoness across the Himalayas. Small, deeply atmospheric and still living, with two ancient orange trees that fruit year-round in the courtyard.

items.name: Drukgyel Dzong
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
items.description: The romantic ruin at the head of the Paro valley, built in 1649 to mark victory over Tibetan invaders and now being carefully reconstructed. On a clear morning the sacred peak of Jomolhari fills the horizon behind it.

items.name: Paro town & weekend market
items.description: A single handsome main street of traditional painted shopfronts, easy to stroll for textiles, thangkas and hand-woven kira. The riverside market brings in valley farmers with red rice, dried chillies, cheese and wild honey.

items.name: Chele La Pass
credentials: Highest motorable pass in Bhutan
items.description: Bhutan's highest motorable pass at 3,988 metres, an hour's spectacular drive from Paro through spruce and larch to a ridge draped in thousands of prayer flags. On a clear day the sacred Jomolhari and Jichu Drake stand out to the northwest; short walks lead to higher viewpoints.

items.name: Kila Nunnery
credentials: Among Bhutan's oldest nunneries
items.description: One of Bhutan's oldest nunneries, a cluster of retreat houses tucked into the cliffs just below Chele La and reached on a serene forest walk. The 20-odd nuns keeping it feel a world away from the tourist circuit.

items.name: Traditional farmhouse visit & hot-stone bath
items.description: Tea, ara and a home-cooked meal inside a rammed-earth Bhutanese farmhouse, followed by the classic dotsho: soaking in river water heated by fire-roasted stones and infused with artemisia. A quiet, deeply local evening that the Aman and COMO lodges also stage beautifully.

items.name: Archery (datse) demonstration
credentials: Bhutan's national sport
items.description: Watch or try Bhutan's national sport, where teams loose arrows at a target a improbable 145 metres away and celebrate each hit with song and dance. Many guides can arrange a friendly local match near Paro.

items.name: Dumtse Lhakhang
items.description: A rare chorten-shaped temple near Paro, built in 1421 by the iron-bridge saint Thangtong Gyalpo and, by legend, once chained down so it would not fly to heaven. Inside are some of the finest and most complete Buddhist wall paintings in the country.

items.name: Zuri Dzong hike
items.description: A gentle 1.5-hour walk to Bhutan's oldest dzong, past a cave where Guru Rinpoche is said to have meditated, ending on a ridge with a full bird's-eye sweep of the Paro valley. The rewarding alternative for those who want a view without the Tiger's Nest climb.

items.name: Jomolhari base-camp trek (start point)
credentials: One of Bhutan's classic high-Himalayan treks
items.description: The classic Himalayan trek to the foot of Bhutan's most sacred 7,326-metre peak begins in the upper Paro valley, threading yak pastures and remote hamlets. For the fit traveller it is one of the great multi-day walks of the eastern Himalaya.

items.name: Buddha Dordenma
credentials: Among the largest Buddha statues in the world
items.description: A 51-metre gilded-bronze Shakyamuni Buddha seated above the capital, housing more than 100,000 smaller Buddhas within. The terrace commands the whole Thimphu valley and is especially moving at first light.

items.name: Tashichho Dzong
credentials: Seat of Bhutan's government and central monastic body
items.description: The gleaming white fortress-monastery on the Thimphu river that houses the throne room, government ministries and the central monk body. Its scale and craftsmanship set the standard for Bhutanese architecture, and it glows under floodlight at night.

items.name: National Memorial Chorten
items.description: The most-visited religious landmark in central Thimphu, built in 1974 in memory of the third king. From dawn, elderly locals circle it clockwise turning prayer wheels; it is the most human, living portrait of Bhutanese faith you can witness.

items.name: Motithang Takin Preserve
credentials: Home to Bhutan's national animal, the takin
items.description: A forested reserve on the edge of the capital devoted to the takin, Bhutan's improbable national animal, a creature that looks assembled from a goat and a cow. A short, easy, kid-friendly stop with real curiosity value.

items.name: Folk Heritage Museum
items.description: A restored three-storey rammed-earth farmhouse that recreates rural Bhutanese life of a century ago, room by room. The most tangible way to understand how most Bhutanese still live outside the towns.

items.name: Royal Textile Academy & National Textile Museum
items.description: Bhutan's finest showcase of weaving, where the extraordinarily intricate kira and gho fabrics that clothe the nation are displayed and demonstrated on the loom. Essential for anyone who values craft, and a discreet place to acquire heirloom-grade textiles.

items.name: Changangkha Lhakhang
credentials: Oldest temple in the Thimphu valley
items.description: A 12th-century fortress-temple on a ridge above Thimphu, the oldest in the valley, where local families bring newborns to be named and blessed. The ramparts give a lovely panorama over the capital.

items.name: Thimphu weekend market
items.description: A riverside pavilion that fills Thursday to Sunday with farmers from across the country: red rice, fiery dried chillies, discs of fresh datshi cheese, ferns, pickles and southern wild honey, plus a handicraft section across the footbridge. The best single window onto everyday Bhutan.

items.name: The giant prayer wheel at Memorial Chorten & Zilukha
items.description: Enormous copper-and-gold mani wheels, each packed with millions of printed mantras, that pilgrims turn to release blessings with every rotation. Spinning one in the flow of chanting elders is a small, grounding ritual you will remember.

items.name: Simply Bhutan living museum
items.description: A hands-on 'living museum' where you try the national dress, archery, butter-tea and folk song in a recreated village setting. Touristic but genuinely fun and a gentle, engaging option for children and grandparents.

items.name: Sangaygang viewpoint
items.description: A short drive to a hillside at 2,685 metres below the telecom tower, giving the classic full-valley view of Thimphu framed in prayer flags. A ten-minute stop that reorients the whole capital for you.

items.name: Cheri Monastery hike
credentials: Site of Bhutan's first monastic community (1620)
items.description: A steep, quiet hour's climb across a covered bridge to the 1620 monastery where Bhutan's unifier established the first monastic body. Deeply peaceful, often shared only with monks and grazing goral on the slopes.

items.name: Tango Monastery hike
items.description: A 90-minute forest walk to a serene 13th-century Buddhist college north of Thimphu, still a place of retreat and study. Pairs naturally with Cheri for a full, unhurried day in the upper valley away from the crowds.

items.name: Dochula Pass & the 108 chortens
items.description: The 3,100-metre pass on the road east from Thimphu, crowned by 108 Druk Wangyal chortens built by the Queen Mother and, on a clear morning, a jaw-dropping line-up of the eastern Himalayan snow peaks. The mountainside cafe here is the classic tea stop en route to Punakha.

items.name: Punakha Dzong
credentials: On Bhutan's UNESCO Tentative List (Bhutanese dzongs)
Often called Bhutan's most beautiful dzong
items.description: Widely held to be the most beautiful dzong in Bhutan, standing at the confluence of the 'father' and 'mother' rivers and blazing purple with jacaranda in spring. Built in 1638, it was the old capital and remains the winter home of the central monk body; the coronation and royal wedding were held here.

items.name: Chimi Lhakhang (the fertility temple)
items.description: A small 1499 hilltop temple reached on a gentle walk through rice terraces and a village painted with phalluses, dedicated to the irreverent 'Divine Madman' saint Drukpa Kunley. Couples come from across Bhutan and abroad for a fertility blessing; the walk itself is one of the loveliest in the west.

items.name: Punakha suspension bridge
items.description: At around 160 metres, one of the longest suspension bridges in Bhutan, swaying gently over the Po Chhu river and hung with prayer flags. A short, exhilarating crossing with dzong and river views, and a fine spot for photographs.

items.name: Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten walk
items.description: A beautiful 45-minute walk across the valley floor and up through pine forest to an elaborately painted royal chorten completed in 1999. The rooftop gives the finest panorama over the terraced Punakha valley and its winding rivers.

items.name: Punakha valley & river
items.description: At around 1,200 metres, warm, low and green, this is where Bhutan slows down: rice paddies, riverside luxury camps and gentle raft floats on the Mo Chhu past the great dzong. The most relaxed leg of a western Bhutan trip, ideal for multi-gen travellers.

items.name: Mo Chhu river rafting
items.description: A gentle scenic float down the Mo Chhu, passing the Punakha Dzong from the water with kingfishers and the occasional heron along the banks. Soft-adventure that suits families and non-paddlers alike.

items.name: A tshechu festival
credentials: Bhutan's most important religious festivals
items.description: The great annual masked-dance festivals, held in dzong courtyards, where monks in brocade and carved masks enact the triumph of dharma over chaos before the whole valley in its finest dress. The Paro Tshechu (spring) and Thimphu Tshechu (autumn, the country's largest) are the most spectacular; dates follow the lunar calendar, so plan the trip around them.

items.name: A monk's blessing
items.description: A private audience or blessing from a lama in a working temple, the thread of blessed cord tied at the neck and butter lamps lit for one's family. In a country where faith is woven into daily life, it is often the moment travellers remember most.

items.name: Guided meditation & mindfulness
items.description: Sunrise meditation in a monastery or lodge shrine room, led by a monk or the resident wellness team at Amankora, Six Senses or COMO. In the last Himalayan Buddhist kingdom this is the natural centrepiece of a slow, restorative trip.

items.name: Ema datshi & Bhutanese cuisine
credentials: Ema datshi is Bhutan's national dish
items.description: The national dish is ema datshi, whole chillies stewed in soft cheese, eaten with nutty red rice, and the wider table is unusually kind to vegetarians, with cheese, ferns, buckwheat and mushrooms everywhere. A cooking demonstration or farmhouse lunch turns a meal into an experience.

items.name: Haa Valley
credentials: Among Bhutan's least-visited valleys
items.description: One of Bhutan's least-visited valleys, reached over Chele La, where the pace slows, homestays and farmhouses replace hotels and the twin white-and-black temples of Lhakhang Karpo and Lhakhang Nagpo anchor the valley floor. For travellers who have seen the icons and want the road less travelled.

items.name: Blue poppy & rhododendron season
credentials: Blue poppy is Bhutan's national flower
items.description: In late spring the high slopes around Chele La and the passes blaze with rhododendron, and the elusive blue poppy, Bhutan's national flower, appears above the treeline. A quiet draw for keen walkers and photographers timing the trip to May and June.

items.name: Amankora circuit
items.description: Aman's five intimate lodges in Paro, Thimphu, Punakha, Gangtey and Bumthang let you travel valley to valley without leaving the brand, with private guides, farmhouse dinners and hot-stone baths arranged throughout. The benchmark for a seamless ultra-luxury Bhutan journey.

items.name: Six Senses Bhutan lodges
items.description: A parallel five-lodge route across the west, each property designed around a distinct valley theme, with standout spas and dramatic architecture at Thimphu ('flying farmhouse') and Punakha. A strong choice for wellness-led, design-conscious travellers.

items.name: COMO Uma Paro & Punakha
items.description: COMO's two hilltop retreats above Paro and in the Punakha valley pair the group's celebrated wellness and cuisine with a warmer, more relaxed feel than the grander houses. Often the best value at the top of the market and excellent for families.

items.name: Punakha to Gangtey (Phobjikha) extension
credentials: Winter roost of the endangered black-necked crane
items.description: A day's drive east of Punakha opens the glacial Phobjikha valley, the winter home of the rare black-necked cranes that arrive from Tibet each November and the graceful Gangtey Goenpa monastery above the wetlands. The natural next step for those extending beyond the west.

items.name: Bukhari
credentials: COMO Uma Paro, Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards 2018
items.description: Named for the Himalayan wood-burning stove at its heart, this circular pavilion at COMO Uma Paro is Bhutan's best-known table, local produce, elegant technique, the valley all around.

items.name: Amankora dining
credentials: Amankora, MICHELIN Key 2025 (Two Keys)
items.description: Quiet, seasonal Bhutanese and Western cooking within the Aman lodges, private, unhurried, and part of the journey rather than a separate outing.

items.name: Six Senses lodge dining
credentials: Six Senses Bhutan, MICHELIN Key 2025 (One Key)
items.description: Wellness-led 'Eat With Six Senses' cooking across the lodges, garden produce, Bhutanese flavours, and a sustainability ethos that runs to the plate.

items.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
credentials: World Culinary Awards 2024, Bhutan's Best Restaurant
items.description: Traditional Bhutanese home cooking in a 500-year-old rammed-earth farmhouse, ema datsi, red rice, the real thing, loved by locals.

items.name: Amankora & lodge bars
credentials: Genuine standing, the bars of Amankora (MICHELIN Key, Two Keys) and the other grand lodges; the considered heart of a Bhutan evening
items.description: In Bhutan the evening happens at the lodge, a fireside single malt, local Bumthang wine or an ara nightcap, in perfect stillness, is the country's idea of a night out.

items.name: Bukhari bar, COMO Uma Paro
credentials: Genuine standing, the bar at COMO Uma Paro (Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice 2018)
items.description: A quiet, elegant drink beside the wood-burning stove that gives Bukhari its name, the most polished bar setting in the Paro valley.

items.name: Mojo Park
credentials: Genuine standing, Thimphu's best-known live-music venue, on Chang Lam
items.description: Thimphu's live-music institution since 2011, local and visiting bands, an easy crowd of Bhutanese and expats, and the closest the capital comes to a real night out.

plan.heading: 5 days in Paro & Thimphu, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The mountain landing into Paro, then a slow settling-in and lunch at your lodge in the valley.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Rinpung Dzong and the old cantilever bridge, then the National Museum in the round watchtower above.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Como Uma Paro or Six Senses, quiet ema datshi and red rice by the fire.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The long walk up to Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery on its cliff, paced with rests and a mid-way tea house.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Descend and rest, then a hot-stone bath to ease the legs.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An early, restorative dinner at the lodge with an early night.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive to the capital, stopping at Simtokha Dzong, then the great seated Buddha Dordenma above the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The weekend market or the National Textile Museum, and the memorial chorten among the prayer wheels.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Six Senses Thimphu overlooking the valley, or a chef's table at Babesa village restaurant.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Up to the Dochula pass and its 108 chortens, the Himalayan range laid out on a clear morning.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Back in Thimphu, the painting school and a papermaking workshop, choosing pieces slowly.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet dinner and an early rest before the return.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Return to Paro for the Kyichu Lhakhang, one of Bhutan's oldest temples, walked in the morning calm.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A farmhouse lunch and a short walk through terraced fields before packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at the lodge, the valley darkening, before the morning flight.

items.name: Paro Valley
items.description: Airport, Tiger's Nest and rice fields; scenic and calm, the classic first base.

items.name: Thimphu
items.description: The capital, Bhutan's only city, for markets, the dzong and a night of dinner and craft shopping.

items.name: Punakha
items.description: Lower, warmer valley beyond the pass; suits an extra day for the dzong and river walks.

events.name: Paro Tshechu
events.note: Masked dances at Rinpung Dzong, closing with the dawn unfurling of the giant Guru Thongdrel tapestry.

events.name: Thimphu Tshechu
events.note: The capital's grand festival in the courtyard of Tashichho Dzong; dates follow the lunar calendar.

events.name: Punakha Drubchen & Tshechu
events.note: A dramatic re-enactment of a 17th-century battle precedes the tshechu at Punakha Dzong.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Thimphu sits near 2,300 m and Paro's Tiger's Nest hike climbs higher, so pace the first day for altitude; dress is modest with covered shoulders and knees for dzongs and temples, and Bhutan levies a daily Sustainable Development Fee handled within your arrangement.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Paro (PBH), one of the world's most demanding approaches, flown only in daylight by Drukair or Bhutan Airlines, where your licensed guide and private vehicle meet you, as all visits are pre-arranged through a local operator.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private vehicle with driver and your assigned guide accompany you throughout by law; the hour's drive between Paro and Thimphu is straightforward and scenic.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: TashiCell or B-Mobile eSIMs give workable 4G in Paro and Thimphu; wifi is reliable in the better lodges, thinner in the valleys and on trekking routes.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Ngultrum (BTN), pegged one-to-one with the Indian rupee, which is accepted directly; cards work at high-end lodges but carry cash, and tipping your guide and driver at the end is customary.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: March to May brings spring blooms and clear valleys, and September to November offers crisp air and the best mountain views; both are the kind seasons. Avoid the June to August monsoon (rain, cloud, flight delays) and the deep cold of December to February.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Paro (PBH) is served only by Drukair and Bhutan Airlines, with daily direct flights from Delhi (~2h30m) and Kolkata; from Mumbai/Bengaluru connect via Delhi or Kolkata. Both carry a business cabin. Seats are limited and the mountain approach is spectacular, so book early and request a left-side window for Everest views inbound.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations; routine jabs plus Hep A advisable. Paro sits at ~2,200m and Thimphu ~2,320m, so mild altitude effects are possible on arrival, take the first day gently. Very safe and low-crime. Drink bottled water; a Sustainable Development Fee applies per day.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Straightforward for vegetarians; Bhutanese cuisine is chilli-and-cheese heavy but every hotel offers Indian and vegetarian options, and the Indian community is well served. Jain travellers should notify lodges in advance, as onion/garlic-free cooking needs prior arrangement; luxury lodges (Amankora, Six Senses) accommodate readily.
